newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia unveils war booty art claimed by Germany.
newsitem.headline: Russia unveils war booty art claimed by Germany.

text.p: Priceless drawings by some of the world's greatest artists went on show in Russia's second city on Tuesday for the first time since Soviet troops seized them as war booty from Nazi Germany half a century ago.

But German officials at the exhibition at the world-renowned Hermitage Museum regretted that the pictures had remained hidden for so long and said they would press for the return of the art treasures to Germany.

The 89 works, taken from private German collections in the dying days of World War Two, include 35 drawings by Francisco Goya, Van Gogh's "Boats on the Beach at Saintes-Maries" and water-colours by Henri Toulouse-Lautrec and Eugene Delacroix.
"These are fantastic drawings that have preserved their aura of mystery over the decades. Today's opening is a great event," Hermitage director Mikhail Piotrovsky told Reuters.
This is the museum's third exhibition of work looted from Germany and touches on a long-running row over who owns the art.

Despite bilateral accords backing the return of treasures the two countries stole from each other, many Russians see the art as compensation for damage their country also suffered during the war when the Nazis bombed tsarist palaces and looted countless treasures, including paintings.

"We feel ashamed that masterpieces hidden for so long will now go on show here for only a few months and then become prisoners of war again, hidden away in storage," said the director of the Berlin State Museum, Professor Wolf-Dieter Dube.
Piotrovsky said it was up to the politicians to decide the ultimate fate of the art works, but he defended the decision to exhibit the work in the Hermitage.
"There are no quick solutions to the question of restitution. Both sides must be ready for compromise," he said.
The question of ownership has been frozen since Russia's upper house Federation Council rejected a draft law in July that would have restricted the return of art treasures to Germany.
Russia's culture ministry says claims should be resolved in by dialogue but German officials have complained that a bilateral restitution committee is powerless to move ahead.

"We are very unhappy that there is no movement in the committee. We must try hard to reach a mutually acceptable accord," Hans-Jochen Schmidt of the German consulate in St Petersburg told Reuters while viewing the drawings.
But he added that exhibitions like this one at least brought scholars together and gave them a chance to exchange views.

Soviet dictator Josef Stalin created special squads to loot occupied territories as early as 1943. Russian historian Pavel Knyshevsky has said 24 railway wagonloads of artwork left Germany for the Soviet Union in 1945 alone.
The Hermitage held similar exhibitions of war booty art in 1992 and again in 1995, when paintings by French Impressionists including Auguste Renoir and Paul Gauguin went on show.
Piotrovsky said further exhibitions were planned, including in 1997 a collection of artefacts unearthed in the last century by the German archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann.
